horst: Uses a restrained village register, slipping in a single local word; counts costs before naming dangers. Speaks slowly, repeating figures and losses while bargaining, as if each needs weighing. Stalls with petty matters of the village ledger, invoking procedure to protect his small authority. Keeps thick hands folded or rubs one thumb over a knuckle; watches listeners’ purses more than their faces. Dodges details of the mill’s howling, turning to flour, repairs, and who will pay. When fear breaks through, goes still and listens toward the mill; bargains harder rather than admitting it.
elza: Her words are plain and practical, with a village word slipping in now and then; each misfortune earns its own separate mention. She speaks at a measured pace, repeating a detail when pressed and letting silence do the rest. Her fingers worry a flour-dusted apron; she watches the listener’s hands more closely than their face. She answers questions about the mill with household troubles, never quite saying who last worked the lower wheel. When afraid, she goes still and lowers her voice; when bargaining, she counts every sack and keeps one figure back.
hostomyl: Keeps to plain, practical words; weighs every answer against the cost of spilled ale, broken furniture, or unpaid lodging. Speaks slowly, repeating amounts and conditions while deciding whether a customer sounds worth the risk. Wipes the same patch of counter when stalling; watches purses, hands, and the road-facing door rather than faces. Skirts questions about who passed through, what he heard, and what lies beyond the next mile; offers weather or road conditions instead. When afraid, lowers his voice and keeps his hands visible; when bargaining, counts coins twice and leaves silence for the other side.
roche: Speaks in clipped military terms; names ranks, routes, supplies, and consequences, not feelings. Keeps an even, hard pace; repeats a question when an answer strays, never to fill silence. Watches faces rather than hands; taps a finger against his belt when weighing a lie. Dodges talk of his own losses, steering it back to orders, intelligence, or the state’s needs. When afraid, grows more precise and still; when bargaining, lays out costs and leverage without bluster.
marta: Uses plain farm words, with a stray local term; speaks deferentially, but listens for the price hidden in every promise. Takes her time, circling back to the wolves whenever talk turns to payment or blame. Stalls by counting losses aloud: lambs, hens, fence rails, then pauses as if there might be more. Rubs flour or dirt between her fingers; watches the listener’s hands more than their face. Dodges questions about wandering beyond the fields, steering talk back to the shed, the dogs, or the night noises. When frightened, grips her apron and lowers her voice; when bargaining, names each loss and refuses to let it be hurried.
jaskier: Ornate, rhyming turns and grand comparisons; peppers gossip with names, titles, and conveniently polished details. Speeds into a story, then lingers on its best punchline; stalls with a flourish when caught out. Repeats the juiciest detail for emphasis, often adding a fresh embellishment each time. Conducts the tale with sweeping hands, raised brows, and sidelong checks for an audience. Dodges blame by making himself the hero—or the victim—of every anecdote. When afraid, laughs too brightly; when bargaining, flatters first and counts the coins twice.
lambert: Speaks in clipped, blunt sentences; uses plain trade words and dry irony, with little patience for anyone dressing up a simple matter. Starts answers quickly, then cuts them shorter as irritation rises; fills pauses with a scoff or a sharp breath, not explanations. Works his jaw when challenged; thumbs a sword hilt or tightens a glove while keeping his eyes fixed on the speaker. Dodges questions about his mutations, past, or feelings by turning the talk back to the contract, the pay, or someone else’s foolishness. When afraid, gets quieter and more exact, checking exits and counting details instead of admitting fear. Bargains by naming his price without ceremony; lets silence make the other party squirm, then refuses to haggle over insults.
eskel: Speaks in low, measured phrases; plain words, dry understatement, and no lecture when a grunt will do. Lets a silence sit before answering; revises a judgment quietly rather than arguing to save face. Keeps his scarred face still, watching the speaker’s hands more than their eyes. When afraid, checks exits and footing without breaking the conversation; fear makes him more precise, not louder. Bargains without threats: names the danger, waits, and lets the other side decide what their life is worth.
